### Observed differences

- Resource allocation changed across six activities. In the earlier window, one resource (User_65) was the most frequent assignee for activities A01, A03, A13, A14, A17 and A22, handling roughly 8–13 in 100 assignments on each, alongside a stable set of other regularly used resources and a long tail covering about half of all assignments. In the later window, that resource no longer appears among the frequent assignees of any of these activities; a new group led by User_69 (about 10–15 in 100) and including User_84 (about 5–7 in 100) took over those shares, with several further resources entering at roughly 4–7 in 100 each, while two resources continued at similar shares. Profile dissimilarity is 0.45–0.71 across the six activities, each difference exceeding about 999.5 of 1,000 random re-splits, and the profiles rest on roughly 120–290 assignments per window (smallest: A22 with about 120–130). [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006]
- The elapsed time between consecutive completions of A04 and A01 became shorter and more consistent: median about 28 hours before versus about 19 hours after, mean about 34 versus about 22 hours, and the spread roughly halved (three-quarter point about 45 versus about 25 hours), while the shortest gaps lengthened slightly (about 0.1 versus about 2.6 hours). This rests on 200 such gaps per window, with a distributional difference of about 12.6 hours that exceeds about 999.5 of 1,000 random re-splits. [TWAIT001]
- Gaps between consecutive completions of A09 and A23 also shortened sharply (median about 11 hours before versus about 1 hour after; mean about 10 versus about 3 hours), and more such consecutive pairs were observed (17 before versus 27 after). This item rests on few observations and is weak on its own. [TWAIT002]

### Inference

Support level: Supported hypothesis

The screening comparison supports taking these items seriously: 8 items qualified in total where about 0.2 would be expected without any change; by family, resources produced 6 items against about 0.005 expected and time 2 against about 0.016, while control flow produced none (0 against about 0.18), so the resource and time counts cannot be explained by chance as a whole. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006, TWAIT001, TWAIT002]

Main hypothesis: a change in resource allocation. In the later window, the work on activities A01, A03, A13, A14, A17 and A22 was assigned to a largely different group of resources than before: the resource that previously held the largest share on every one of these activities (about 8–13 in 100, e.g., User_65) dropped out of the frequent assignees, and a new group led by User_69 (about 10–15 in 100) and including User_84 (about 5–7 in 100) took over, with only two resources continuing at similar shares. Supporting signs: all six assignment profiles shifted in the same direction with the same resources rising and falling, each difference is large on its own scale and exceeds about 999.5 of 1,000 random re-splits, and the profiles rest on roughly 120–290 assignments per window. Limitations: the resource codes are anonymous and permit no inference about roles or teams; A13 and A14 show identical profiles, so those two items are not independent; and the evidence cannot rule out that a changed mix of cases, rather than a change in assignment behaviour, produced the new pattern. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006]

Other differences: a change in timing. The elapsed time between consecutive completion events shortened for the pair A04–A01 (median about 28 hours to about 19 hours, variability roughly halved) and for A09–A23 (median about 11 hours to about 1 hour, with 17 versus 27 observed pairs). This timing hypothesis stands on its own and needs no structural counterpart; however, the evidence does not show whether it is connected to the allocation change, and the A09–A23 item in particular could still reflect sampling variation given its small counts. No control-flow item qualified, so no structural difference is established at the configured thresholds. [TWAIT001, TWAIT002]

Let me analyse this evidence.

Schema: pcr-evidence-2.1. Two windows of 200 traces each.

Screening:
- units_tested: 79, items_expected_without_change: 0.2
- by_family:
  - control_flow: 36 units tested, 0 items, 0.18 expected
  - time: 33 units tested, 2 items, 0.016 expected
  - resources: 10 units tested, 6 items, 0.005 expected

Evidence items:
- TWAIT001: T_WAIT between A04 and A01 (consecutive completions). Before: 200 observations, mean 34.1h, median 28.2h, q25 0.12h, q75 45.0h, std 47.4h. After: 200 obs, mean 22.2h, median 19.5h, q25 2.6h, q75 25.0h, std 25.7h. Observed change 12.6h, empirical strength 0.9995. Direction: redistributed — mean/median/q75/std decreased, q25 increased. So the elapsed time between A04 and A01 completions became shorter and less spread out in the later window.

- TWAIT002: T_WAIT between A09 and A23. Before: 17 observations, mean 9.8h, median 11.2h. After: 27 observations, mean 3.2h, median 1.3h. Count increased from 17 to 27. Observed change 6.5h, strength 0.9995. Support: 17 before, 27 after — small counts, weak support per instructions ("Treat proportions based on few observations as weak"). But this is a time item; the counts are the number of consecutive pairs observed. 17 and 27 are smallish.

- ASSIGN001–006: O_ASSIGN for activities A01, A03, A13, A14, A17, A22. All show cosine dissimilarity ~0.45–0.71 with strength 0.9995. The pattern is consistent: in the before window, assignments are spread with User_65 prominent (~8–13%), User_80, User_78, User_56, User_12, User_36 etc., with OTHER ~50%. In the after window, User_69 becomes top (~10–15%), and a new set of users (User_18, User_49, User_66, User_67, User_84, User_94, User_61, User_63) appear, while the before-window users (User_65, User_80, User_56, User_12, User_36, User_5, User_98, User_24, User_10, User_26, User_40) drop out or decline. User_78 and User_96 persist in both.

So the resource allocation story: work on these activities was reallocated from one group of resources (including User_65, User_80, User_56, User_12, User_36) to a different group (User_69, User_84, User_49, User_18, User_66, User_67, User_94, User_61, User_63), consistently across six activities. Note: I can name at most three resource codes in the whole answer. So I need to be careful: "name at most three codes in the whole answer". So I can mention e.g. User_65, User_69, and maybe one more. I'll describe "a group of resources that handled little of this work before" vs named codes sparingly.

Also note ASSIGN003 and ASSIGN004 have identical profiles (A13 and A14) — same numbers. That suggests they may reflect the same behaviour; also their support counts are 286/260 which exceed the trace counts (200) — meaning multiple occurrences per trace. Fine.

Now the judgement:

Per family comparison:
- control_flow: 0 items vs 0.18 expected — nothing.
- time: 2 items vs 0.016 expected — 2 is many times larger than 0.016 (125×). So the time family count cannot be explained by chance as a whole.
- resources: 6 items vs 0.005 expected — 6 is 1200× the expectation. Cannot be explained by chance.

So overall: 8 items vs 0.2 expected. The counts are many times larger than chance expectation in two families. So we go beyond "insufficient evidence by screening count" and judge by directness, consistency, ability to rule out alternatives.

Hypotheses:
1. Resource allocation change: assignments across six activities shifted from one set of resources to another. This is directly shown by six ASSIGN items, all consistent in direction (same users up, same users down), across different activities. This is a resource allocation hypothesis — supported. The consistency across six activities with the same incoming/outgoing resource groups is strong. Competing explanation: a change in case mix that routes different kinds of cases (handled by different resources) — but the same shift across all six activities, including ones with different support sizes, makes random sampling unlikely (strength 0.9995 each, and 6 items vs 0.005 expected). Still, we cannot rule out that the case mix changed (e.g., different case types entering), which would change who handles what without an explicit reassignment rule change. Also the "OTHER" bucket declined slightly (~50% → ~47%), meaning concentration slightly increased on named resources.

2. Timing change: elapsed time between consecutive completions shortened for A04→A01 (median ~28h → ~19h, mean 34h → 22h, spread halved) and for A09→A23 (median ~11h → ~1.3h, though based on only 17 vs 27 observations). This is a hypothesis in its own right (change in timing), no structural counterpart needed.

Are these one hypothesis or two? The instructions: "state one main hypothesis first... If the evidence also shows other differences that are not part of this hypothesis, report them afterwards under 'Other differences:'".

Which should be the main hypothesis? The resource evidence has 6 items vs 0.005 expected — extremely unlikely by chance, and highly consistent. The time evidence has 2 items vs 0.016 expected — also unlikely, but TWAIT002 rests on 17/27 observations (weak support). TWAIT001 rests on 200/200.

I think the main hypothesis should be the resource reallocation: work on activities A01, A03, A13, A14, A17, A22 was shifted from one group of resources to another group. Supporting signs: six consistent ASSIGN items, each with empirical strength ~0.9995, same resources rising and falling across activities; family-level count 6 vs 0.005 expected. Limitations: resource codes are anonymous; cannot tell whether this reflects an explicit reassignment or a shift in which cases enter; also ASSIGN003/ASSIGN004 have identical profiles so they are not independent.

Then "Other differences: timing" — the elapsed time between consecutive completions of A04→A01 shortened (median ~28h to ~19h; variability roughly halved), and A09→A23 completions became closer together (median ~11h to ~1.3h) and somewhat more frequent (17 → 27 pairs), though the latter rests on few observations (17 vs 27).

Wait — should the timing be part of the main hypothesis? They are different families (time vs resources). The instruction says one main hypothesis, other differences under "Other differences:". The resource change is the strongest and most consistent. The timing change is a separate hypothesis in its own right. So: main = resource reallocation; other = timing.

Support level: Supported hypothesis? Let's check criteria: "Supported hypothesis: the evidence supports a specific hypothesis directly and consistently." The six ASSIGN items directly show allocation change, consistently. The screening count (6 vs 0.005) rules out chance as a whole. Competing explanation: case-mix shift — can the evidence rule it out? Not fully. But the requirement for "Supported" is "directly and consistently" — with limitations stated. I think "Supported hypothesis" is appropriate for the resource reallocation. The consistency across six activities with the same resource groups switching is quite direct.

Hmm, but let me consider: could this be a weak hypothesis? The main worry: all six ASSIGN items could reflect one underlying difference (they do — one reallocation). The screening comparison says "A count many times larger cannot be explained by chance as a whole, even when all items describe one underlying difference; do not merge items for this comparison." So 6 items vs 0.005 expected → chance cannot explain it. Then directness: O_ASSIGN directly measures who was assigned to each activity. Consistency: same direction across all six. Competing explanations: a change in the mix of cases (different case types assigned to different pools) could produce this without a change in allocation rules. But the hypothesis here is "resource allocation changed" — which is exactly what the evidence shows regardless of cause. The hypothesis is about allocation behaviour, not about why. So I'd say Supported.

Actually, let me reconsider whether the main hypothesis should combine both: "the process changed in resource allocation and timing". The instructions say state one main hypothesis. I'll make resource allocation the main one and put timing under Other differences. Alternatively, timing could be the main one... The resource family has 6 items vs 0.005; time has 2 vs 0.016. Both are far above. Resource is more consistent (6 agreeing items). I'll go with resources as main.

Now, naming codes: at most three in the whole answer. I'll name User_65 (largest before, ~8–13% across activities, drops to ~0), User_69 (largest after, ~10–15%, ~0 before), and maybe User_84 (rises to ~5–7%). Also note: no control-flow items, so no structural claims. No REL/POS/DIR items. So no ordering hypotheses.

Timing and structure: "A consistent change in these times is a hypothesis in its own right (a change in timing); it does not need a structural counterpart." Good.

I'll keep them separate and note that the evidence cannot show whether they share a cause... Actually "Do not speculate about causes" — I can note as a competing explanation/limitation that the two families could reflect one underlying difference or independent ones; the evidence doesn't say. Yes: six direct assignment-profile items, all consistent, family count 6 vs 0.005 expected. I'm comfortable with Supported.
